content: Progestogen-only pills (POPs), also known as progestin-only pills or mini pills, are contraceptive pills that contain synthetic progestogens (progestins) but do not include estrogen. Despite sometimes being referred to as progesterone-only pills, they do not actually contain natural progesterone but rather chemically related compounds. There are various formulations of progestogen-only contraceptives available. Mechanism of Action The contraceptive effect of progestogen-only pills depends on the activity and dosage of the progestogen. Very low-dose progestogen-only contraceptives (such as traditional mini pills, subdermal implants like Norplant and Jadelle, and intrauterine systems like Progestasert and Mirena) inconsistently inhibit ovulation, doing so in approximately 50% of menstrual cycles. Their primary mechanism of action is thickening the cervical mucus, which reduces sperm viability and penetration. Intermediate-dose progestogen-only contraceptives (such as the pill Cerazette or the subdermal implant Implanon) allow some follicular development but inhibit ovulation more consistently, in 97–99% of cycles. These also cause the same cervical mucus changes as very low-dose progestogens. High-dose progestogen-only contraceptives (such as injectable forms like Depo-Provera and Noristerat) completely suppress follicular development and ovulation. They also induce the same cervical mucus changes as the lower-dose formulations. In anovulatory cycles induced by progestogen-only contraceptives, the endometrium becomes thin and atrophic. If the endometrium is similarly thin and atrophic during an ovulatory cycle, it could theoretically interfere with the implantation of a blastocyst (embryo). Efficacy The theoretical efficacy of progestogen-only pills is comparable to that of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs). However, POPs are taken continuously without breaks between packets, and traditional mini pills must be taken at a much stricter time each day (within a 3-hour window, compared to the 12-hour window for COCPs). In some countries, the POP Cerazette has an approved 12-hour window. The real-life efficacy of POPs is highly dependent on user compliance. Unlike COCPs, POPs do not rely on gut bacterial flora for absorption and are therefore not affected by antibiotic use. However, their effectiveness can be compromised by episodes of diarrhea or vomiting. Benefits Since progestogen-only pills lack estrogen, they are not associated with an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or heart disease. The reduced clotting risk makes them suitable for use in individuals with sickle cell disease. The absence of estrogen and the low dose of progestogen make POPs safe for use during breastfeeding, and they may even enhance milk production. Like combined pills, POPs reduce the likelihood of pelvic inflammatory disease. However, it is unclear whether POPs provide the same level of protection against endometrial and ovarian cancers as COCPs. Side Effects With continuous dosing, menstrual flow does not initially occur at predictable intervals. Over time, most women experience light spotting at approximately regular intervals. POPs may cause mastalgia (breast tenderness) or mood swings. Weight gain is less commonly reported with POPs compared to COCPs. Breast Cancer Risk Epidemiological evidence regarding the relationship between POPs and breast cancer risk is less conclusive than for COCPs, as studies have involved smaller populations of POP users. A large 1996 reanalysis of hormonal contraceptive studies included less than 1% of POP users. This analysis found a slight, non-statistically significant increase in breast cancer diagnoses among POP users. As with COCPs, any increased relative risk of breast cancer diminishes over time after stopping use and disappears after 10 years. This pattern is consistent with the possibility of earlier diagnosis or the promotion of growth in preexisting cancers. The most recent (1999) International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) evaluation of progestogen-only contraceptives reviewed the 1996 reanalysis and four case-control studies of POP users. The IARC concluded that there was no evidence of an increased risk of breast cancer with progestogen-only contraceptives. However, due to inadequate evidence, they classified POPs as possibly carcinogenic. Concerns about the role of progestogens in the increased breast cancer risk associated with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in postmenopausal women, as observed in the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trials, have not extended to the use of progestogen-only contraceptives in premenopausal women.
